title: He Asked Followers for Diwali Sweets. They Sent a ₹1.69 Lakh TV — on Cash-on-Delivery
excerpt: Madurai creator Veeramani shared his address for a box of sweets and was flooded with fake COD orders for TVs, fridges and phones, until appeals failed and he left home.
body:
• Madurai humour creator Veeramani shared his home address and phone number online asking followers to send him a box of Diwali sweets; pranksters instead placed cash-on-delivery orders in his name.
  • Delivery riders from Amazon and Flipkart arrived with televisions, refrigerators, washing machines and smartphones — one TV was priced at ₹1.69 lakh — none of which he had ordered or could pay for.
  • Veeramani posted a video appeal asking people to stop, said switching his phone off or on both caused problems, and eventually left his home in the Anuppanadi area as deliveries continued.
  • The costs of fake COD orders fall on delivery workers and sellers, who travel, wait and absorb return logistics for purchases that never existed.

Veeramani, a social media creator from Madurai known for humour videos in local slang, wanted a box of sweets for Diwali. He posted his address and phone number and asked followers to send some. What arrived instead was a procession of delivery riders carrying televisions, refrigerators, washing machines and smartphones — all ordered cash-on-delivery in his name, all unwanted, and all demanding payment at his door.

How a sweet request became a siege

According to Livemint, Veeramani had previously asked followers for financial help — he raised about ₹6,000 toward a trip to Kerala, which he then documented. The Diwali appeal repeated the pattern with a smaller ask. But once an address and phone number are public, anyone can place a COD order against them: no payment is verified upfront, and the doorstep becomes the point of failure. One fake order was reportedly for a television worth ₹1.69 lakh. Veeramani could neither pay nor produce the one-time passwords delivery staff requested, and Tamil reports described food deliveries from Swiggy and Zomato arriving alongside the appliances.

"I fall at your feet. Please stop placing orders."

— Veeramani, in a video appeal to followers

The appeal, then the exit

In videos posted online, Veeramani said the orders kept coming whether his phone was on or off, and that he had no money to pay for any of them. Dexerto reported he eventually left home as the stream of riders continued; reporters who later visited found the house locked, with neighbours confirming he had gone. He said he was also thinking of the delivery workers, who travel long distances only to find a recipient who never ordered anything.

The wider lesson, five days before Diwali

The episode is a compact demonstration of why personal details should never be posted publicly, even for the most benign reason. COD remains a large share of Indian e-commerce, and its trust model — pay at the door — makes a named address a usable weapon: the prank costs the sender nothing, while the recipient, the rider and the seller absorb the time, fuel and return shipping. Platforms can and do block abusive ordering patterns, but only after the fact. For the diaspora sending Diwali gifts home this week, the same system works the other way: order prepaid, confirm with the recipient, and never ask anyone to publish an address to receive a gift.
